name: Rosa Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing primary teaching, so my week is lectures on child development, a school visit on Wednesdays, and a lot of reading. I live in halls on the edge of the city, in a corridor with eleven other people and one very small kitchen. Saturday and Sunday I work at the cinema café, mostly making coffees and sweeping popcorn. My parents pay my halls fees between them, and I cover food and everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that AI is helpful for small things, like tidying a lesson plan, but it won't run a classroom. I'd say it's a tool and we shouldn't panic. And I'd say schools need proper funding more than they need gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it changes very little for me, which is a relief. What bothers me is money: my dad drives a bus and my mum is a care assistant, so my parents are stretched already. If the prices of everything keep creeping up, their help with halls might not last the whole degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cinema job and use AI the way I do now, which is for summarising long readings. I'd apply for the faculty hardship fund if I needed it, and I'd start putting the school-visit notes in a folder so I'm ready for placements. That's about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about AI, more about whether my family can hold on financially. I love my course, so that part feels good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum works in a care home. How does that shape your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum has done twelve-hour shifts for years and gets paid barely above the minimum. My mum works in a care home and she's exhausted, so my main worry is her wage and her back, not any robot. She says I should be a teacher so I never have to lift anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in your own first years of teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan. The student loan will be around forty thousand by the end, and starting salaries in schools aren't huge. I'd also worry about a class of thirty children with one adult and not enough support staff.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool** and schools need real funding more than gadgets.
think: The change is small for me, but my parents' **money** is already stretched.
I worry their help with **halls fees** might not last the whole degree.
do: Keep the **cinema café** job on weekends.
Use AI only to **summarise** long readings.
Apply to the faculty **hardship fund** if money gets tight.
feel: A bit **uneasy** about my family's money, and happy about my course.
S0.quote: My mum works in a care home and she's exhausted, so my main worry is her wage and her back, not any robot.
fieldNote: Her worry is her **parents' income**, not technology, which keeps her uneasy even when nothing changes.
Already a light AI user and sees it as a **study aid**.
Pride in a degree that her mother's tiring work made possible.

steps.text: Keep working weekends at the cinema café
Use the AI summariser for long course readings
Apply to the faculty hardship fund if halls help stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools should be careful. Marking, planning and report writing could be done by software, and that should give teachers time back for children, not be a way of cutting jobs. I'd say unions and the government need to decide that together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think teaching is quite safe, because parents want a person in the room with their six-year-old. But the school budgets could be squeezed, with software as the excuse for fewer teaching assistants. I'd be happy to learn the tools, since I'm already using them a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools properly now rather than now and then, and I'd ask my tutors which ones schools actually trust. I'd also volunteer at a primary school on Fridays so I know the real work. And I'd try to join the student teachers' union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. The routine bits of the job I don't love, like paperwork, so I'd be glad of help. The thing I'd hate is a school treating teaching assistants as cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a teacher's job could software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lesson plans, marking spelling tests, writing reports, emailing parents. All the things that eat evenings. If software does the paperwork, teachers should get to spend the time with the children, not lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum that care work isn't going anywhere because people need people. But she should still push for decent pay, because the software might change how her home is run and who gets hired.

say: I'd say software should give teachers **time back**, not cut jobs.
I'd say unions and government must decide it **together**.
think: Teaching feels **safe** because parents want a person in the room.
I fear budgets will use software as an excuse to cut **assistants**.
do: Use AI tools **properly** and ask tutors which ones schools trust.
Volunteer at a **primary school** on Fridays.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, since paperwork is the part I like least.
S1.quote: If software does the paperwork, teachers should get to spend the time with the children, not lose their jobs.
fieldNote: Sees real **benefit** in handing paperwork to software but worries about how schools will use the savings.
Her plan is **practical**: more AI use, more classroom time, a union.
Connects her mother's care job to the same question of **who benefits**.

steps.text: Try the AI planning tools my tutors say schools trust
Join the student teachers' union branch this term
Volunteer in a primary classroom every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and we aren't ready, and that the government must step in now. I'd say it's not a time for the usual arguments. I'd also say we have to look after children in schools, because they're the ones inheriting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. Two years means I'd be in the middle of my course when it happens, and no one can say what a teaching degree is worth then. Teaching may last longer than office jobs, because it's people, but classes could shrink or be taught partly by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course, since quitting would waste the year, and I'd get more placement time. I'd save every bit from the cinema job and cut spending to the basics. I'd also talk to the faculty about what they are planning, and ask my parents to be honest about what they can keep paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with moments of feeling calm because I'm busy. It's the not knowing that gets me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years differ from ten for someone who is just starting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I could try other things and watch how schools react. With two, there's no spare time, so I'd have to commit to teaching, lean on my parents and keep my costs low. Two years doesn't give me time to change my mind, so I'd have to stay on my course and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that we should look after what we have: keep the savings, don't take on new debt, and I'll cover more of my own costs. And I'd tell them that I'll manage, even if I'm not sure, because I don't want them lying awake.

say: I'd say the government must **step in now** and protect schools.
I'd say children are the ones **inheriting** this.
think: I'm **anxious** because no one can say what my degree will be worth.
Teaching might outlast desk jobs, but classes could shrink or use **software**.
do: Stay on the course and ask for more **placement time**.
Save the cinema wages and cut spending to **the basics**.
Ask my parents what they can **keep paying**.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly at night, with some calm when I'm busy.
S2.quote: Two years doesn't give me time to change my mind, so I'd have to stay on my course and hope.
fieldNote: The **short window** removes her chance to experiment, so she commits to staying put.
She protects her parents from **worry**, which tells you how close she is to them.
Her plan is **modest**, built on saving and placements.

steps.text: Stay on the teaching course and add extra placement days
Save all the cinema café wages each month
Cut spending to food, transport and phone only
Ask my parents what halls help they can keep paying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough runway if people use it. Schools, teacher training and governments should start now, and I'd ask my university what they're changing in the course. I'd tell my friends to keep learning the tools and not to hide from this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years in a classroom before AGI, so I'd at least be in a job. The scary part is that by 2034 robots might handle some classroom support, and I don't know what's left for teachers. I'd like to think children still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a permanent post in a state school, and put away a few hundred a month for a cushion. I'd take a short course in using AI in the classroom. I'd also start learning a second subject I could teach, like maths or special needs, in case classes change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anything. There's time, so it isn't panic, but I'd keep thinking about it on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in a five-year window that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In five years I could actually do the cushion and the extra qualification, and see teaching first-hand before deciding. With five years I could save a cushion and get a second qualification, which isn't possible if it all happens in two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it was time to change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If schools in my area started letting teachers go or merging classes, I'd think about special needs teaching, which seems harder to automate. I'd also ask my mum about care roles, since that's a field I know a bit about from her.

say: I'd say five years is a **long enough runway** if people use it.
I'd tell friends to keep learning the **tools**.
think: I'd have about **two years** in a classroom before the thinking AI arrives.
I don't know what's left for teachers once **robots** arrive.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **permanent post** in a state school.
Save **a few hundred** a month for a cushion.
Study a second subject, such as **special needs**.
feel: **Uneasy** but not panicked, since I'd have time to act.
S3.quote: With five years I could save a cushion and get a second qualification, which isn't possible if it all happens in two.
fieldNote: Time lets her plan a **second qualification**, which she sees as a hedge.
Her private **dread** is what teachers do once robots arrive.
Practical and steady, as her profile says.

steps.text: Finish the primary teaching degree and apply to state schools
Put aside a few hundred a month once I'm teaching
Take a special needs teaching course by third year
Do a short course on using AI in the classroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time to get this right, and we should use it. I'd tell friends to keep their eyes open but get on with life. I'd also say governments shouldn't waste it arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm about it. I'd have about seven years as a teacher before AGI and probably a family by then. The robots in 2039 are far enough that I'd treat it like pensions: something to plan for, not lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, teach, and learn the AI tools as schools adopt them. I'd save for a home, and I'd get involved in the union so teachers have a say in how the tools come in. I'd keep an eye out for new kinds of school roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, and a bit curious. Ten years is enough to build a career and a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop worrying about with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money worries about my parents would still be on my mind, but my own career wouldn't. I'd stop fretting about whether my degree is wasted, because I'd have a long run at the work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still prepare for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still keep saving and keep up with the tools. Ten years is a long time, but I'd still save a little every month, because the people who are caught out are the ones who didn't prepare.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if we use it well.
I'd tell friends to **get on with life**.
think: I'd teach for about **seven years** before AGI and probably have a family.
I'd treat it like **pensions**, something to plan for.
do: Finish the degree and **teach**, learning AI tools as schools adopt them.
Get involved in the **union** so teachers have a say.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time, but I'd still save a little every month, because the people who are caught out are the ones who didn't prepare.
fieldNote: Ten years turns the scenario into a **planning** problem for her.
Still carries **concern** for her parents' finances.
Her steady, practical style comes through in the pension comparison.

steps.text: Finish the degree and start teaching in a state school
Learn each AI tool as my school brings it in
Save monthly towards a deposit for a home
Join the teachers' union so staff help shape new tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be in the middle of my degree and my parents' money is already tight. What would help is honest information from my university about the degree's worth, and extra support for students whose families can't help much. A guaranteed placement would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm proud to be the first in my family at university, and I'd hate for this to feel like it was wasted. I wouldn't change anything about my choice, but I'd want someone to tell me the truth.

headlineQuote: I'm proud to be the first in my family at university, and I'd hate for this to feel like it was wasted.
portrait: Rosa is a 19-year-old **primary teaching** student, living in halls and working weekends at a cinema café.
Her dad drives a bus and her mum works in a care home, so **family money** is always on her mind.
She uses AI now and then, and is practical about it, not frightened or excited.
She is **uneasy** when little changes, anxious in the two-year world, and calm when she has ten years.
She plans with savings, placements and a second qualification, and she protects her parents from worry.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world, when she'd be mid-degree and her parents' money is tight.
whatWouldHelp: Honest information from her university about what her **degree** will be worth.
Extra **support** for students whose families can't help much.
